analysis.one_liner: Denies presidents and vice presidents immunity from federal criminal prosecution and limits Supreme Court review.
analysis.headline: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar in September 2024 but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Responding to the Supreme Court's July 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, this bill declares that no president or vice president is entitled to any immunity from federal criminal prosecution unless Congress grants one. It bars courts from treating a president's alleged crimes as "official duties," and it strips the Supreme Court of the power to dismiss such prosecutions or to strike down the bill itself, channeling any constitutional challenge through the D.C. district court and D.C. appeals court only. It passed no chamber; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday citizens who rely on the principle that no one, including the president, is above criminal law. If a future president or vice president committed a federal crime while in office, prosecutors could pursue the case in ordinary federal courts, and neither a claim of immunity nor an emergency Supreme Court intervention could shut the prosecution down. State criminal prosecutions remain untouched and explicitly preserved.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens, and the rule of law

how_it_helps.text: Declares that a president, former president, vice president, or former vice president has no immunity from federal criminal prosecution unless Congress specifically grants one, directly rejecting the Supreme Court's holding that presidents have at least presumptive immunity for official acts.

Bars courts from dismissing an indictment, halting a grand jury, overturning a conviction, or otherwise stopping a criminal case against a president or vice president on the ground that the act was an official duty — the route by which the immunity ruling could protect a prosecuted president.

Removes the Supreme Court's ability to intervene in such prosecutions or to declare the bill unconstitutional, sending any challenge only through the D.C. district court and D.C. appeals court with strict deadlines and a requirement that the law be presumed valid unless proven otherwise by clear and convincing evidence.
Explicitly preserves state criminal prosecutions, so the federal change does not limit states' ability to hold a former president accountable under state law.

analysis.who_pays: Presidents, vice presidents, and former officeholders, who would lose the immunity from federal prosecution that the Supreme Court recognized in July 2024 and could face criminal charges for conduct in office without the official-acts shield. The Supreme Court itself would lose jurisdiction it currently exercises over these cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Presidents and vice presidents, past and future

drawbacks.text: The bill strips the Supreme Court of appellate jurisdiction over these cases and over challenges to the bill itself; many constitutional scholars argue Congress cannot remove the Court's power to decide the constitutionality of a federal law in this way, so the core provisions could well be struck down as unconstitutional if they were ever tested.

It was written in direct response to one Supreme Court ruling and one pending prosecution, which invites the criticism that it was tailored to a political fight of the moment rather than a neutral, general rule — a weakness opponents could cite even if the underlying principle finds support in history and the Federalist Papers.

The compressed timelines (a 180-day window for facial challenges, 90 days for as-applied challenges) and the presumption of constitutionality are unusual devices; critics would say stacking procedural rules to shield a law from review undermines normal checks and balances even when the goal is accountability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core goal — that no president is above the criminal law — reflects the Constitution's original design and the near-universal expectation of ordinary citizens, and the bill already preserves state prosecutions, so the downside for the public is limited. The serious cost is design, not aim: the attempt to wall off Supreme Court review is legally aggressive and would likely fail in court, meaning the bill might not survive even if enacted. A narrower bill that simply codified criminal liability for presidents without the jurisdiction-stripping machinery would have been more durable, but would also have been easier for courts to neutralize through the immunity doctrine again.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate put the bill on its calendar in September 2024, but the Senate — including the bill's own sponsor, who was the majority leader and controls what gets a floor vote — never brought it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on August 1, 2024, about a month after the Supreme Court's ruling granting presidents immunity for official acts; 36 senators, all Democrats or independents, signed on as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on September 9, 2024 — a step that makes it eligible for floor action but commits the Senate to nothing.
No floor debate, vote, or committee action followed; the bill sat on the calendar until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

With 37 supporters out of 100 senators, all from one party, the bill would also have needed substantial Republican support to clear the Senate's 60-vote threshold to end a filibuster, and no Republican ever signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Presidents and former presidents are better off: the Supreme Court's immunity ruling stands as the operative law, and no statute limits it. The Supreme Court also keeps the final word over presidential immunity questions that the bill would have taken away.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidents shielded by the Court's immunity ruling

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and read it twice to place it on the Senate calendar, but never scheduled it for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

for.name: 36 Senate cosponsors
for.role: All 36 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, including Sens. Durbin, Warren, Klobuchar, Sanders, and Booker
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original or early cosponsors of the immunity-stripping bill; none was a Republican.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: The Republican conference, in the minority
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it far short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster and bring it to a final vote.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: As the senator who controls the floor schedule, placed the bill on the calendar but never called it up for debate or a vote in the roughly four remaining months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely one-sided: all 37 initial supporters were Democrats or independents, with zero Republican cosponsors, and the bill never reached a vote where any crossover could have occurred.

industries.industry: Presidents, vice presidents, and former officeholders
industries.note: The bill would have removed the immunity from federal criminal prosecution that the Supreme Court recognized for official acts, exposing current and former presidents and vice presidents to ordinary criminal process. That exposure is the point: the public's interest in accountability runs against the officeholder's interest in protection.

industries.industry: The Supreme Court as an institution
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the Court's appellate jurisdiction over presidential-immunity criminal cases and over challenges to the bill itself. Defenders of the Court's role would see this as Congress weakening a constitutional check; the bill's supporters see it as Congress reclaiming authority over a ruling it considers wrong.
